items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Two engines, one fuel: AI capex (+0.5pp) and the equity wealth effect (+1pp) now carry most US growth
items.idea: Guatieri estimates AI hardware/software/data-centre spend added ~0.5pp to real GDP over the year to Q3 net of imported equipment, while the equity wealth effect added ~1pp — in an economy growing just over 2%. Both engines are exposed to the same shock: an equity drawdown hits consumption and AI return expectations simultaneously.
items.angle: Roughly 70% of US growth is now market-derived. That makes the equity tape a macro variable, not just a price — this week's -8.6% SPX week is a GDP input.
items.tweetA: 1.5pp of ~2.1% US growth comes from two things: AI capex and people feeling rich from stocks. Both run on the same tape. SPX just had a -8.6% week. That's not a market story anymore, that's a Q1 GDP story.
items.tweetB: The bull case for 'resilient economy' quietly assumed the market keeps going up. BMO's math says ~70% of growth is market-linked. Resilience was collateralised by the S&P. $SPY $XLY

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: BMO lifts Q4 GDP to 2.3% after Q3's 3.4% — while pending home sales hit the weakest since 2001
items.idea: BMO raised Q4 GDP to 2.3% annualized after a 3.4% Q3, and keeps 2.4% for 2027. Meanwhile residential permits are at the lowest since the pandemic and pending home sales the weakest since at least 2001 — but residential construction is under 4% of GDP, so housing can collapse without derailing the aggregate.
items.angle: Housing is the textbook transmission channel for rate hikes and it is already broken — yet it's too small to matter. The Fed's lever is working on the wrong 4% of the economy.
items.tweetA: Pending home sales: worst since 2001. GDP: 3.4% and tracking 2.3%. The Fed is hiking into an economy where its main transmission channel is already dead and too small to matter. So what does it break next to get inflation down? Equities.
items.tweetB: Housing <4% of GDP, at a 25-year low in activity. AI capex + wealth effect ~1.5pp of growth, at record highs. If you want to know what the Fed actually has to slow, it's not homebuilders. $XHB $ITB

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: The 50bp hike scenario: BMO flags 'unusually aggressive' Fed tightening — and the self-limiting feedback loop
items.idea: Guatieri explicitly raises the possibility of 50bp Fed hikes. His escape valve: a deep enough equity decline makes the Fed cautious, long yields fall, weaker demand pulls oil lower and inflation eases — meaning a correction need not become a downturn. But several adverse shocks arriving close together could overwhelm momentum.
items.angle: The 'Fed put' is now conditional on equities falling enough first. That's a put struck well below spot — the market must do the Fed's tightening for it.
items.tweetA: The Fed put still exists. It's just struck about 15% below where we started. BMO's own scenario: stocks fall enough → Fed blinks → long yields drop. That's a curve steepener with a lot of pain in the middle. $TLT
items.tweetB: Either 50bp hikes come and equities fall further, or equities fall further and 50bp hikes don't come. Notice both paths start the same way.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Anthropic's $81B IPO pushes 2026 US IPO proceeds above $230B — nearly 2x the 2021 record
items.idea: Total US IPO proceeds exceeded $230B in 2026 vs the prior record of ~$120B in 2021. Kavcic shows 2026 is the strongest year for IPO fundraising relative to S&P 500 market cap since 2000 — but dot-com era volumes were often 2-3x larger on that same scaled basis.
items.angle: Anthropic alone is ~35% of the entire year's IPO proceeds. Supply of AI equity is the under-discussed driver: the market just had to absorb $230B of new paper into a tightening cycle.
items.tweetA: One company raised $81B. That's ~35% of every US IPO dollar in a record year, and ~2/3 of the entire 2021 record by itself. When a single issuer is the market, 'IPO boom' is the wrong frame — it's a supply shock. $SPY
items.tweetB: $230B of new equity supply in a year the Fed is hiking. Everyone asks who's selling AI stocks. Nobody asks how much new AI stock had to be bought. The float expanded right into the top.

charts.desc: IPO proceeds as % of S&P 500 market cap by year: 2026 highest since 2000, but 1999-2000 bars 2-3x taller — the 'it's not 1999 yet' chart

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Not 1999: ~900 IPOs in 1999-2000 vs <100 in 2025; 1999 average day-one pop >70%
items.idea: Kavcic contrasts composition: nearly 900 companies listed in 1999-2000, many with questionable models, versus fewer than 100 in 2025 — today's market is a few enormous deals. Retail frenzy is muted: Anthropic faded after its debut and SpaceX sat ~30% below its opening-day high, versus >70% average equal-weighted day-one returns in 1999.
items.angle: Concentration cuts both ways: fewer junk companies, but the risk is now in a handful of mega-floats owned by everyone through indices.
items.tweetA: 1999: 900 IPOs, average day-one pop 70%. 2026: a handful of mega-deals, SpaceX 30% under its opening high, Anthropic down 9% on day two. The bubble isn't in the number of companies. It's in the size of three of them.
items.tweetB: The 'not like dot-com' argument is that IPOs are concentrated. That's also the bear argument. In 2000 you could avoid Pets.com. In 2026 the index buys Anthropic and SpaceX for you.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Your 'diversification' into industrials, utilities, materials and financials is the same AI bet with a different label
items.idea: Kavcic: gross AI infrastructure investment added ~1pp to real GDP before imports (vs Guatieri's ~0.5pp net). The cycle has spread into industrials (data-centre construction), utilities (generation/distribution), materials (copper) and financials (debt/equity financing). The top-10 S&P names are ~40% of the index.
items.angle: Sector labels are stale as risk factors. A real AI-hedge needs to be built on factor exposure (power, copper, capex-linked credit), not GICS.
items.tweetA: Top 10 = 40% of the S&P. Then you rotate into utilities (data-centre load), industrials (data-centre builds), copper (data-centre wiring) and banks (data-centre loans). Congratulations on your diversified AI portfolio. $XLU $XLI $FCX
items.tweetB: The gap between gross (1pp) and net (0.5pp) AI GDP contribution is imports — half the capex leaks to Taiwan, Korea, Mexico. Which means an AI capex cut hurts $TSM and $EWY GDP more than US GDP.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Households: equities ~50% of financial assets, ~25% of total assets — both above the late-1990s peak
items.idea: Stocks and funds are almost 50% of US household financial assets and ~25% of total assets, both records exceeding the dot-com peak. Higher-income households hold most of it and drive discretionary spending, so the wealth effect now runs both ways with unprecedented leverage to the tape.
items.angle: The K-shaped consumer is a market-beta consumer at the top. Watch luxury, travel and premium credit-card spend as the real-time read of the drawdown.
items.tweetA: US households have more of their net worth in stocks than at the 2000 peak. S&P is -11.6% from its high. Do the arithmetic on the top decile's 'feeling rich' budget before you buy luxury and travel into Black Friday. $LVMUY $BKNG
items.tweetB: Record equity share of household assets means the Fed's tightening now transmits through brokerage statements, not mortgages. Powell isn't raising your borrowing cost. He's lowering your 401(k).

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Kavcic: the AI boom is itself causing the Fed tightening that will end it
items.idea: Kavcic argues the hiking cycle is tied to AI: infrastructure absorbs capital, labour, electricity and physical resources, sustaining inflation and keeping policy restrictive. Loop: AI capex → profits → equities up → consumption up + inflation → tighter policy → higher financing costs → challenges the capex that started it.
items.angle: This is the 'AI is inflationary' thesis in official-economist form — a reversal of the 'AI is deflationary' consensus. It argues for real assets and against long duration even in an AI slowdown's early phase.
items.tweetA: For two years the pitch was 'AI is deflationary.' BMO now says AI capex is a reason the Fed is hiking. Electricity, copper, electricians, concrete. The productivity comes later. The inflation came first.
items.tweetB: A reflexive loop with a central bank in the middle: AI capex → inflation → hikes → AI financing costs up → capex cut. The only question is whether the cut comes from a CFO or a credit market. $HYG

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / BMO Economics (Guatieri, Kavcic)
items.title: Week ahead: headline PCE could hit 3.8% y/y, core 3.2%; BMO expects a December hike and more in early 2027
items.idea: BMO's Scott Anderson sees October personal income +0.3%, spending +0.4%, core PCE +0.3% m/m and 3.2% y/y, and headline PCE near 3.8% y/y — real income growth near stagnant. He expects a December hike, possibly followed by more early 2027. Durables expected +0.5% (core +0.4%); Beige Book watched for equity-weakness spillover — lower-income households are trading down.
items.angle: A 3.8% headline print in a week where SPX is in correction sets up the cleanest test of whether the Fed prioritizes inflation or markets.
items.tweetA: Headline PCE 3.8%. Real incomes flat. Stocks in correction. Fed expected to hike anyway. If Wednesday's print lands hot, the 'Fed put' crowd has to explain why it hasn't shown up at -11.6%.
items.tweetB: Everything lands Wednesday before Thanksgiving: PCE, GDP, durables, claims, Beige Book. Thin liquidity, maximum data. The Beige Book line I'd look for: 'higher-income consumers pulling back.' That's the wealth effect turning.

items.tweetA: SPX gave back an entire year in a week. +10% YTD a week ago, +0.76% now. RSI 24. The first bounce will feel like the bottom. The 200-day at 7,350 is where we find out. $SPY $ES_F
items.tweetB: Nasdaq -10% in a week and now -2.7% YTD. The Anthropic IPO bounce lasted a morning. When the best AI news of the year can't hold an intraday rally, the problem isn't news. It's positioning. $QQQ

items.title: BTC wicked to $55,266 through the June-July lows, then reversed on well-above-average volume
items.idea: BTC at $60,361 is 21.8% below its 50SMA, 16.7% below its 200SMA, RSI 23.35, -31.98% YTD. items.tweetA: $BTC swept the June-July lows to $55.3K on a Saturday and got bought on heavy volume. Weekend undercuts of obvious lows are where stops get harvested. Close above $58K and that was the low. Close below and it was a preview.
items.tweetB: BTC -32% YTD. Gold -18% YTD. Both 'debasement trades' are breaking at the same time the Fed is hiking. That's not a coincidence — it's what happens when the thing you were hedging (easy money) reverses.

items.tweetA: $SOXX was +43% YTD a week ago. It's +18% now. Highest volume candle in its history. Capitulation volume, but still a lot of 2026 profit left on the table for someone to take. $NVDA $SMH
items.tweetB: Semis back to the exact $123 level that capped February. Old resistance → new support is the cleanest test there is. Hold and this is a reset. Lose it and February's base becomes the target.

items.title: Gold $3,537: -8.92% week, -18% YTD, 20% below the 200SMA — author eyes a 200-week retest to add physical

items.tweetA: Gold 20% below its 200-day is a level you see maybe once a decade. Even gold bulls are saying 'wait for the 200-week.' When the holders won't buy, you haven't found the bottom yet. $GLD
items.tweetB: Gold -18% YTD while the Fed hikes and the dollar rips. Remember when 'central banks will never let gold fall' was the thesis? Central banks buy on a schedule. Margin clerks sell on a clock. $GDX

items.tweetA: $EEM fell more than the S&P this week (-11.6% vs -8.6%). EM is a levered bet on Taiwan and Korea semis plus a weak dollar. This week gave you the opposite of both.
items.tweetB: EM death cross incoming. The Fed hiking 50bp into a global selloff would be the most EM-hostile setup since 2022. If you're looking for where the next funding stress shows up, look east. $EWT $EWY

items.source: SixSigmaCapital / Preview of the Week Ahead
items.title: Breadth collapse: S&P stocks above 50DMA from 71.8% to 43.2% in one week
items.idea: The share of S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day moving average fell to 43.20% from 71.80% the prior week — a 28.6-point drop in five sessions, with 4 distribution days on SPX.
items.angle: Breadth fell from healthy to washed-out in one week, which typically marks crash-like liquidation rather than a slow topping — those more often produce sharp reflex rallies.
items.tweetA: 71.8% → 43.2% of S&P stocks above their 50-day in ONE week. That's not a rotation, that's a liquidation. And 43% isn't even washed out yet — capitulation lows usually print under 20%.
items.tweetB: Breadth went from 72% to 43% in five days. Index -8.6%. If the average stock is still above its 50-day nearly half the time, the generals got shot first. The soldiers haven't been asked yet.

items.title: Lilly under distribution: new high $1,475 Monday, then down every day, RSI negative divergence
items.idea: LLY made a new high of $1,475.25 on Monday (author trimmed at $1,460), then closed lower every session, -6.68% on the week, on rising above-average volume Wed-Fri. RSI made a lower high while price made a higher high; it closed below the 5EMA and 21EMA. Still +25.45% YTD, 20.8% above its 200SMA.
items.angle: LLY was the hiding place. When the crowded defensive growth winner starts distributing, the de-grossing is moving from AI into everything that worked.
items.tweetA: $LLY made an all-time high on Monday in the worst week since 2020. Then sold off every day after. When the last place to hide starts getting sold, de-grossing has moved from 'sell AI' to 'sell what worked.'
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching NVDA. Meanwhile $LLY, +25% YTD and the market's favourite non-AI growth story, is showing textbook distribution — higher high, lower RSI, rising volume on down days.

items.title: Mega-cap tape: META -12.6% below its 200SMA, MSFT trimmed to market weight, AMZN holds the 200-day

items.tweetA: $META -12.6% on the week, $MSFT -7.3%, $AMZN -7.4% but held its 200-day to the penny. The market is starting to grade hyperscalers on who can monetize capex. META is getting the worst grade.
items.tweetB: Practitioners are trimming $MSFT to market weight, not zero. That's the tell: nobody wants to be overweight the AI capex payer, but nobody wants to be short the moat either.

items.title: Biotech loses its last support: XBI breaks the 200SMA, still +15.5% YTD
items.idea: XBI held its 200SMA through Thursday but lost it Friday, finishing -6.89% on the week at $140.18; it has now lost all key moving averages. Bulls want a quick reclaim of $143.39. Still +15.47% YTD.
items.angle: Biotech is the most rate-sensitive growth sector; a hiking cycle with 50bp risk should pressure it more than it has — the YTD cushion is the vulnerability.
items.tweetA: $XBI lost its 200-day. Biotech is long-duration cash flows funded by capital markets — the exact thing a 50bp hike and a $230B IPO supply glut compete with. +15% YTD is a lot to give back.
items.tweetB: Rate hikes + equity drawdown + IPO window clogged by AI megadeals. If you're a pre-revenue biotech needing a raise in Q1, the window just shrank. Watch follow-on offering discounts. $XBI

items.title: Thanksgiving compression: PCE, Q3 GDP, durables, claims and the Beige Book all land Wednesday Nov 25
items.idea: Calendar: Mon Flash PMIs + Fed's Williams; Tue Conference Board confidence; Wed Oct PCE/income, Q3 GDP second estimate, October durables, jobless claims (brought forward), Beige Book; Thu closed; Fri early 1pm ET close.
items.angle: Stacking the week's entire data load into one pre-holiday session with thin liquidity is a volatility event in itself.
items.tweetA: Five macro releases plus the Beige Book in one session, the day before markets close, after a -8.6% week. Wednesday is the most dangerous day of the month and half the desk will be on a plane.
items.tweetB: Williams speaks Monday. He's the NY Fed — closest to the market. If he doesn't push back on 50bp after an 8.6% week, that's the signal the Fed is fine with stocks doing the tightening.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs (Robert Quinn)
items.title: Gold's $600 collapse in nine sessions: -9% Nov 17-20, below $3,600 for the first time since Sept 2025; silver -15%
items.idea: Gold fell ~9% from Nov 17-20 and ~10% on the week, below $3,600 for the first time since September 2025; silver lost ~15%. The decline far exceeded what the rate repricing (Waller floating a 50bp December hike) and dollar strength would explain — and gold sold off alongside tech even as oil fell and growth assets buckled.
items.angle: Gold trading as a risk asset correlated with tech is the signature of a funding liquidation, not a fundamental re-rating — those historically reverse faster than macro-driven selloffs (cf. March 2020, Oct 2008).
items.tweetA: Gold just fell $600 in nine sessions and traded tick-for-tick with Nasdaq. When the safe haven correlates with the thing you're fleeing, it's not a safe haven. It's the ATM. $GLD $SLV
items.tweetB: March 2020: gold -12% in 8 days on margin calls, then +40% in 5 months. Oct 2008: same pattern. Liquidation lows in gold are violent and short. The question isn't 'why did gold fall?' It's 'who's left to sell?'

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs (Robert Quinn)
items.title: Goldman's Robert Quinn: 'Margin Calls and Volatility Stress' — gold sold because investors need cash, not because the thesis died
items.idea: Goldman futures trader Robert Quinn's research argues the selloff moved beyond macro into forced liquidation: investors aren't abandoning gold's fundamental appeal, they're selling it to meet margin calls. The author notes the fundamental reasons to own gold have changed little; the speculative excess may now be flushed.
items.angle: Forced sellers create the best entry prices — but the timing depends on when the equity margin calls stop, i.e. gold's bottom is downstream of the Nasdaq bottom.
items.tweetA: Goldman's futures desk says gold isn't being sold, it's being raised — as in, raised as cash. Gold's bottom isn't a gold call. It's an equity margin call call. Watch $QQQ to time $GLD.
items.tweetB: The thesis for gold (debt, deficits, central bank buying) didn't change in nine days. The holders' leverage did. Those are different problems with different half-lives.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman Sachs (Robert Quinn)
items.title: 4-5 sigma moves in gold options: 3M implied vol jumps to 27.6 from ~19, 25-delta skew re-prices violently
items.idea: On Nov 20, three-month gold implied volatility and normalized 25-delta put-call skew moved ~4-5 standard deviations. 3M IV surged toward 27.6 from ~19 at end-October. Quinn frames it as the contrarian signal: extreme protection pricing has historically signaled seller exhaustion.
items.angle: IV +45% in three weeks with puts bid makes selling gold puts / buying call spreads the asymmetric trade if you believe the liquidation thesis.
items.tweetA: Gold 3M vol 19 → 27.6 in three weeks, +45%. Put skew moved 4-5 sigma in one day. When protection is this expensive, the asymmetric trade is to sell it, not buy it. $GLD puts are paying you to be patient.
items.tweetB: A 4-5 sigma move in gold skew is a once-in-a-decade event. Either the market knows something structural just broke in gold, or everybody bought the same hedge on the same day. My bet is the second.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: EU 'cut' of €204B still leaves the 2028-34 budget ~25% larger — and makes Big Tech the designated payer via a 3% digital levy
items.idea: Costa cut €204B from the Commission's initial 2028-2034 MFF plan, yet the revised budget remains ~one-quarter larger than the current one. The extra money is assigned to a proposed 3% levy on large digital companies, replacing a blocked corporate-tax idea. Not approved, not in force — model it as a negotiating exposure, not a booked liability.
items.angle: A 3% EU-wide digital levy would be a direct margin hit to US megacaps' European revenues and a fresh US-EU trade-war trigger at a sensitive moment for the AI complex.
items.tweetA: Brussels 'cut' its budget by €204B and it's still 25% bigger. The trick: name a payer who can't vote. A 3% levy on Big Tech's EU revenue. $GOOGL $META $AMZN — this is a margin line, not a headline.
items.tweetB: The EU's new funding model: expand spending, assign the bill to US tech. With Washington already in tariff mode, a 3% digital levy is a trade war fuse with a 2028 timer.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: COP31 goes into overtime after fossil-fuel language vanishes from the draft — EU warns of a 'fossil summit'
items.idea: Negotiations at COP31 ran past deadline after fossil-fuel commitments disappeared from the draft text; the EU warned the meeting risked becoming a 'fossil summit.' Separate energy discussions placed high prices ahead of broader climate ambition. Fulcrum links it to Costa's logic: cost politics beats ambition.
items.angle: Climate policy is visibly subordinating to energy affordability — supportive for upstream oil & gas capex duration and negative for policy-dependent renewables multiples.
items.tweetA: COP31 quietly deleted fossil fuels from the draft. When energy prices are high, the climate summit becomes an affordability summit. That's a policy regime change for $XLE vs $ICLN.
items.tweetB: Gasoline $3.69 vs $3.10 a year ago, and the climate negotiators just blinked. The voter's energy bill now outranks the 1.5°C target in every capital. Price that into renewables subsidies.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: FBI investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center database
items.idea: U.S. media, citing two people briefed, report the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of NCIC — the central criminal-justice database queried by law enforcement nationwide (warrants, stolen property, missing persons, watchlists).
items.angle: A compromise of the core law-enforcement database is a national-security cyber event; it lands in a week of 'technology outages' disrupting banking and travel — tailwind for federal cyber spend.
items.tweetA: The FBI's NCIC — the database every US cop queries for warrants and watchlists — may be breached. Same week as outages hitting banks and airlines. Federal cyber budgets are about to get a lot less debatable. $CRWD $PANW $ZS
items.tweetB: If NCIC is compromised, the damage isn't data theft — it's integrity. Can you trust a warrant hit? Cyber's next market is not protecting data, it's proving data wasn't altered.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: Trump bars federal contractors from disclosing information to Congress without White House instruction — after Democrats win sweeping midterm majorities
items.idea: Per Politico, President Trump barred federal contractors from sharing information with Congress absent explicit White House instruction, following Democrats' sweeping midterm wins.
items.angle: This sets up an oversight collision with defense/government-services contractors caught between subpoenas and executive orders — headline and legal risk for the GovCon sector into 2027.
items.tweetA: Democrats win Congress. Days later, federal contractors are told not to talk to Congress without White House sign-off. If you own defense or GovCon names, you now own a subpoena-vs-executive-order fight. $LMT $BAH $PLTR
items.tweetB: The 2027 oversight playbook just changed: Congress can't easily go through agencies, so it'll go after contractors. And contractors just got an order not to answer. That's a constitutional fight priced at zero.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: EU and Indonesia sign a market-opening trade agreement, expected in force early next year
items.idea: The EU and Indonesia signed a market-opening trade deal in Brussels, expected to take effect early next year.
items.angle: Indonesia is the world's dominant nickel producer and a key battery/stainless supply node; an EU deal reshapes critical-mineral access and Indonesia's export-ban leverage.
items.tweetA: EU-Indonesia trade deal signed. Indonesia controls roughly half of global nickel supply. Brussels just bought a critical-minerals relationship while Washington fights tariffs. $VALE
items.tweetB: While the US tariffs everyone, the EU is signing FTAs with Mercosur-era urgency: now Indonesia, 280M people. Trade diversion is the quiet second-order effect of US tariff policy.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih kills two, wounds 58
items.idea: A Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih — Ukraine's iron-ore and steel hub, Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two and wounded 58, per Zelenskyy.
items.angle: Kryvyi Rih is a major iron-ore/steel center; continued strikes there are a quiet input to European steel supply and reconstruction-play valuations.
items.tweetA: Kryvyi Rih isn't a random target — it's Ukraine's iron ore and steel heart. 58 wounded in one strike. The war's economic geography matters for European steel more than the headlines suggest.
items.tweetB: The war barely registers on markets anymore while Nasdaq falls 10% a week. That's exactly when geopolitical tail risk gets mispriced — attention is a finite resource.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: US Army to detonate nearly five tons of deteriorating explosives in Iowa after canceling chemical-neutralization contract
items.idea: Per the NYT, the US Army plans to open-detonate nearly five tons of deteriorating explosives at an Iowa base after canceling the contract to neutralize them chemically.
items.angle: Aging munitions stockpiles and disposal shortcuts are a quiet signal about the state of US munitions logistics — the same industrial base being asked to replenish for Ukraine and Middle East.
items.tweetA: The Army is blowing up five tons of deteriorating explosives in Iowa because the contract to neutralize them was cancelled. The US munitions industrial base can't even dispose of old stock cleanly. Replenishment is the bigger problem. $GD $NOC
items.tweetB: Nobody's talking about this: legacy munitions are degrading faster than they're being replaced or safely disposed. That's a defense budget line item, a local environmental fight, and a readiness question at once.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (Fulcrum)
items.title: French court recognizes racist nature of police violence against Michel Zecler; three officers sentenced 1-2 years
items.idea: A French court recognized the racist nature of three police officers' violence against music producer Michel Zecler and sentenced them to one to two years in prison.
items.angle: A judicial finding of racism in a police case is rare in France and could feed into policing reform politics ahead of the 2027 presidential race.
items.tweetA: A French court explicitly named racism as the motive in a police beating — rare in a country that officially avoids racial categories. Watch how it plays into the 2027 presidential campaign's law-and-order debate.
items.tweetB: France doesn't collect ethnic statistics, so courts rarely name race. This ruling does. Small headline, but it's a legal precedent in a country where the far right is polling to win in 2027.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: S&P -11.6% from the Oct 6 record, tech -~25%, seven straight losses — longest streak since Feb 2020
items.idea: The S&P 500 is down 11.6% from its October 6 record, the tech sector has shed nearly a quarter of its value, and the index fell seven consecutive sessions — its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Dow joined the S&P in correction. Anthropic surged Thursday, gave back its debut enthusiasm, then fell another 9% Friday.
items.angle: Tech -25% vs SPX -11.6% means the non-tech 70% of the index is roughly flat-to-mildly-down — the economy-level stress is still ahead if Black Friday disappoints.
items.tweetA: Tech -~25%. S&P -11.6%. Do the math: ex-tech, the index is barely down. The market has priced an AI correction. It has not priced a consumer one. Black Friday is the test. $XLK $XLY
items.tweetB: Longest S&P losing streak since February 2020. Anthropic -9% the day after its record IPO. When the best possible AI catalyst can't stop the selling, you're not in a news market. You're in a flow market.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Holiday sales +4.2% nominal, +2.2% real: the gap between spending more and buying more
items.idea: Oxford Economics expects Nov-Dec holiday retail sales (ex autos, gas, bars, restaurants) +4.2%, but only ~2.2% in real volume. NRF expects 182.7M Thanksgiving-to-Cyber-Monday shoppers, down from 186.9M last year. October core retail sales beat; Walmart and Target were constructive.
items.angle: Implied ~2% goods inflation vs ~3.8% headline PCE: inflation is in services/energy, not the checkout aisle — retailers can't price their way to margin. Fewer shoppers (-2.2%) spending more each = concentration in higher-income households, which the equity drawdown hits directly.
items.tweetA: NRF: 4.2M fewer Black Friday-weekend shoppers than last year (-2.2%). Sales still +4.2% nominal. Fewer people, bigger tickets. That's the top-decile consumer — the same one whose portfolio just fell 11%. $WMT $TGT $AMZN
items.tweetB: Holiday sales: +4.2% nominal, +2.2% real → ~2% goods inflation. Headline PCE: 3.8%. Inflation isn't on the shelf, it's in rent, insurance and energy. Retailers have no pricing power to hide behind. Margins are the swing factor. $XRT

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Gasoline $3.69: down 14% in a month from $4.28, still 19% above a year ago
items.idea: US gasoline averaged $3.69/gal Friday, down from $4.28 a month earlier but well above the $3.10 of a year ago. Together with food and borrowing costs, it squeezes household budgets into the holiday season.
items.angle: A 14% m/m gas drop is a meaningful tailwind for November/December headline CPI and real incomes — it partly offsets the wealth-effect hit and gives the Fed a reason to skip 50bp.
items.tweetA: Gas fell from $4.28 to $3.69 in a month. That's a ~$0.60/gal tax cut landing right before Black Friday, and a headline CPI drag the Fed will see in December. Nobody's pricing the disinflation in the pump. $XLE $UGA
items.tweetB: Gas +19% YoY but -14% MoM. Consumers feel the level ($3.69 vs $3.10). The Fed sees the change. Those two are about to diverge — sentiment stays sour while headline inflation rolls over.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Wall Street Week Ahead
items.title: Recent technology outages hitting banking, travel and email are compounding AI-trade anxiety
items.idea: The note flags recent technology outages disrupting banking, travel and email as an added sentiment drag — a reminder of how dependent the economy is on a concentrated set of providers — while investors struggle to separate AI-financing concerns from disorderly liquidation of crowded positions. Dell and Analog Devices report next week.
items.angle: Concentration risk is now operational, not just financial: outages + the NCIC breach make resilience/redundancy spend and observability a budget line in 2027.
items.tweetA: Outages taking down banks, airlines and email in the same month the AI trade unwinds. The market's concentration risk and the economy's concentration risk turned out to be the same handful of providers. $MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Dell and ADI report into this tape. After NVDA's solid print got sold, the bar isn't 'beat.' It's 'raise and explain who's paying.' $DELL $ADI
